newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian markets stabilise after campaign start.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian markets stabilise after campaign start.

text.p: Indonesia's financial markets steadied on Monday after a smooth start to the general election campaign and brokers and dealers said the rupiah and stocks should improve as long as political tensions did not flare up.
Currency dealers said the rupiah staged a strong comeback after falling to an historic low last week against the U.S. dollar on fears of possible campaign violence.
The rupiah recovered about 10 points on Monday.
Stock brokers said the Jakarta composite index gained 4.05 points, or 0.62 percent, to close at 656.53 on Monday, with local buying seen leading the momentum.
Spot rupiah recovered gradually to 2,426.5/27.0 at 0945 GMT against an opening of 2,435.5/36.5 on Monday.

"I think the (stock) index is going to come back. Some people are a little nervous. But I think you would probably find after the first week it's going to be a boring issue if there is no significant (campaign) trouble," one European broker in Jakarta said.
The Sunday campaign launch proceeded peacefully with only a few minor scuffles reported through the archipelago of 200 million people. The election is on May 29.
Saleh Aziz, treasury manager of PT Bank Export Import Indonesia, told Reuters the rupiah was expected to recover gradually if things remained under control.
"I think the rupiah will go back to the bid side of the central bank (intervention) band and people will start to focus on the liquidity issue again," Aziz said.
The band, which is set daily, allows the central bank to intervene in the market if rates fall out of the range.
The intervention band was set at 2,406/2,598 on Monday.
Aziz said it would be difficult for the dollar to touch the 2,440 level again, broken last week after the market factored in possible disruption during the campaign.
The same view was shared by a number of economists polled by Reuters last week about the prospects for the rupiah in the run-up to the elections.
Vincent Low, economist of JP Morgan in Singapore, said he expected further capital inflows into Indonesia on the back of sound economic fundamentals.
"People still like the rupiah. The carry (yield) is good."

Low said the country's core inflation rate -- the non-food components -- was declining, suggesting the underlying inflation trend was doing well. Indonesia's consumer price index fell to 6.47 percent in 1996 from 8.64 in 1995.
Brokers said the stock market had been widely spared after a minor sell-off last Friday, suggesting the turbulence in the foreign exchange market was driven by speculation.
Stephen Doe, head of research at PT Asia Equity Jasereh, said sentiment would very much depend on what happened on the streets during the campaign period.
"If we have more days like yesterday, the market should move up again," said Doe.
"Everybody knows this is one of the best markets in the region. It's the cheapest market with low rating and good earnings growth. It's a good story with the economy."
